headline: Vosoritide
punch: The only approved drug on this list that grows bone.

headline: What it actually is
body: A synthetic analogue of *C-type natriuretic peptide*, given as a daily subcutaneous injection. It binds **NPR2**, also called GC-B, on growth plate chondrocytes and signals through cGMP into PKG. | None of that touches growth hormone or IGF-1. It is a genuinely parallel route into the same tissue, which is why it works in a condition where the GH axis is intact and the problem is elsewhere.
punch: A second pathway, not a GH booster.

headline: Why it releases the brake
body: *FGFR3* puts a brake on chondrocyte proliferation, and achondroplasia is caused by an FGFR3 that is permanently switched on. The obvious target is FGFR3 itself, which is a hard and unselective drug problem. | The cGMP arm of CNP signalling functionally antagonises that brake downstream. So you can release it by pushing the opposing pathway instead of blocking the overactive one.
punch: Release the brake from the other side.

headline: The phase 3 result
body: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, **121 children** with achondroplasia across 24 sites in seven countries, 52 weeks of daily injections at 15 µg/kg. | Adjusted mean difference in annualised growth velocity: **1.57 cm per year** over placebo, 95% CI 1.22 to 1.93, **p < 0.0001**. That is a real randomised human result on a pathway with nothing to do with GH.

headline: Velocity is not height
body: Straight from the paper: **it is not known whether final adult height will be increased, or what the harms of long-term therapy might be**. | Growth velocity measured over one year is a rate, not an outcome. A rate can rise and then be given back later through earlier fusion, and 52 weeks cannot tell you which happened.
punch: A rate is not a final number.

headline: The licence is narrow
body: It is approved for achondroplasia, in children, with open growth plates. The label does not support adult use and there is no trial in anyone with a normal FGFR3. | The whole mechanism is releasing a brake that is pathologically stuck on. In someone whose FGFR3 is behaving normally, there is much less brake to release.
punch: The drug fixes a specific broken thing.

headline: It works where it counts
body: In cartilage-specific CNP knockout mice the **hypertrophic layer was drastically reduced** while the proliferative layer fell only moderately. So this pathway acts mainly on the final swelling stage. | That matters because hypertrophy is described in the Hunziker work as the most efficient cellular process contributing to bone elongation. It is hitting the biggest lever in the plate rather than a peripheral one.
punch: It targets hypertrophy, the strongest lever.

headline: And the signal is local
body: Knock CNP out only in cartilage and the mice come out **almost as short as deleting it everywhere in the body**. The CNP that lengthens bone is made inside the plate, not delivered by blood. | Which is the argument for an analogue in the first place: you are topping up a locally made signal from outside, and the dosing question is how much reaches an avascular tissue.
punch: Same lesson as local IGF-1, different pathway.

headline: The genetics are the floor
subhead: LIMIT · WHY THIS IS NOT SPECULATIVE
body: NPR2 loss of function causes acromesomelic dysplasia and gain of function causes skeletal overgrowth. Carriers of a single broken copy run a height z-score of **-1.8** against **-0.4** in non-carriers, P < 0.0005. | A gene whose dose moves human height in both directions is about as solid a target as this field offers. The uncertainty here is about the drug, not the pathway.
punch: The pathway is proven. The outcome data is one year long.

headline: Verdict
body: The best-evidenced compound on this entire list: randomised, placebo-controlled, in humans, on a pathway with independent genetic support in both directions. | What it does not have is a final-height result, a licence outside achondroplasia, or any data in a normal FGFR3. Treat the mechanism as settled and the extrapolation beyond the label as untested.
